lessons.title: Lesson 1: What fintech is and where AI fits
lessons.text:
Lesson 1 of 6 · about 4 minutes
Goal: Name four kinds of fintech and one way each uses AI.
This lesson builds toward: Given the money apps on your phone, you will identify four kinds of fintech and one way each uses AI, and name what you can do when an AI decision about your money is wrong.
Fintech means financial technology: apps and websites for money. Common kinds are mobile banking, payment apps for sending money to people, budgeting apps, online lenders and investing apps.
AI is used behind the scenes: to spot fraud (a card used in two countries in an hour), to answer questions in chatbots, to sort your spending into categories, and to help decide who gets a loan.
AI decisions can be wrong. A real purchase can be blocked, or a loan turned down because of bad data. You have rights to ask why and to dispute mistakes; the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau (CFPB) explains them.
Words to know:
- Fintech: financial technology: apps and websites for banking, paying, borrowing, budgeting and investing.
- Fraud detection: tools that watch for payments that look stolen or fake.
- Chatbot: an AI program that answers questions by chat.
Official sources:
- CFPB: Military financial lifecycle (service members and veterans)
Try it now: List every money app on your phone. Next to each, write which kind of fintech it is and one way it might use AI.
You can now describe the main kinds of fintech and how they use AI.

check.q: Which is a kind of fintech?
options: A paper checkbook
A cash jar at home
A payment app on your phone
A printed bank statement
check.why: Fintech means apps and websites for money, such as payment, banking, budgeting and investing apps.

check.q: Your money app's AI flags your normal rent payment as fraud and blocks it. What do you do?
options: Contact the company, ask why and dispute the mistake
Delete the app and never pay rent online
Share your password so they can fix it
Wait and hope it clears
check.why: When an AI decision about your money is wrong, you can ask why and dispute it.

lessons.title: Lesson 2: Where your money really sits: banks, apps and insurance
lessons.text:
Lesson 2 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Check whether money in an app is protected by FDIC deposit insurance.
This lesson builds toward: For one money app you use, you will check whether money in the app is protected by FDIC deposit insurance, by finding its partner bank and confirming it on FDIC BankFind.
FDIC deposit insurance protects money in deposit accounts (checking, savings, money market deposit accounts and CDs) at an FDIC-insured bank. When we checked fdic.gov in October 2026, the standard amount was at least $250,000 per depositor at each insured bank.
FDIC insurance does not cover stocks, bonds, mutual funds, annuities, life insurance or crypto assets. Many payment apps are not banks. A balance left in the app may not be insured unless the app places it in an insured bank account for you.
To check: read the app's own help page for the name of its partner bank, then look that bank up with the FDIC's BankFind tool on fdic.gov.
Step by step:
- Open the app's help or legal page and look for "FDIC" and a bank name.
- Look up that bank name with FDIC BankFind on fdic.gov.
- Check whether your type of money (deposit, stock, crypto) is covered.
- If you are unsure, move spending money to an insured bank account.
Words to know:
- FDIC: Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation: protects deposits at insured banks if the bank fails.
- Deposit account: a checking, savings, money market deposit account or CD at a bank.
- BankFind: the FDIC's free tool to check whether a bank is FDIC-insured.
Official sources:
- FDIC: Deposit insurance
Try it now: Pick one money app you use. Find its partner bank in the app's help pages and check that bank on FDIC BankFind. Write down whether your balance is insured.
You can now check whether money in an app is protected by FDIC deposit insurance.

options: A loan app
A crypto exchange
A credit score tool
The FDIC's tool to check whether a bank is insured
check.why: BankFind lets you confirm that a bank is FDIC-insured.

check.q: A payment app says your money is "safe". How do you check whether it is insured?
options: Trust the app's ad
Find its partner bank in the help pages and look it up on BankFind
Ask the AI assistant
Assume all apps are banks
check.why: Insurance depends on whether the app holds your money at an insured bank, which you confirm on BankFind.

lessons.title: Lesson 3: How robo-advisors and crypto work, and their risks
lessons.text:
Lesson 3 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Explain how a robo-advisor and crypto work and name their main risks.
This lesson builds toward: When you hear about a robo-advisor or crypto, you will explain how each works and list its main risks, checking the risk list against an official source such as the FTC.
A robo-advisor is an app that uses computer rules to put your money into investments based on answers you give, such as your goals and how long until you need the money. It charges a fee. Investments can lose value, and they are not FDIC-insured.
Crypto (cryptocurrency) is digital money recorded on a shared online ledger called a blockchain. Prices can rise and fall sharply. The FTC warns that crypto payments usually cannot be reversed and crypto is not insured by the government the way bank deposits are.
This course does not tell you whether to use either one. Before any investing decision, learn the fees and risks on official pages and talk to a qualified, independent professional or a free military or VA financial counselor.
Words to know:
- Robo-advisor: an app that invests money using computer rules based on your answers.
- Cryptocurrency: digital money recorded on a blockchain.
- Blockchain: a shared online record of transactions that is very hard to change.
- Volatile: a price that can go up and down a lot, fast.
Official sources:
- FTC: What to know about cryptocurrency and scams
- FDIC: Deposit insurance
Try it now: Ask an AI assistant: "Explain how a robo-advisor works and how crypto works, in simple words, with the main risks of each." Check its risk list against the FTC crypto page and write down anything it missed.
You can now explain how robo-advisors and crypto work and name their main risks.

options: It invests using computer rules based on your answers
A person at the bank picks stocks for free
It guarantees your money grows
It is the same as a savings account
check.why: A robo-advisor uses computer rules and your answers to invest; it carries market risk.

check.q: A friend says crypto is "insured like a bank account". What do you tell them?
options: That is right
Only on weekends
Crypto is not insured like bank deposits and prices can swing sharply
Crypto payments can always be reversed
check.why: Crypto is not insured like bank deposits, its prices can swing, and payments usually cannot be reversed.

lessons.title: Lesson 4: Checking an app before you trust it
lessons.text:
Lesson 4 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Run a five-point check on a money app before you put money in it.
This lesson builds toward: Before you put money into an app, you will run a five-point check on the app, writing yes or no for every point.
Scammers build fake money apps and websites that look real. Before you download or deposit, check who runs the app and whether it is real.
Get the app only from the official app store and check the developer name matches the real company. Read the company's own website for its full name and its partner bank. Check FDIC BankFind for the bank. Search the company name plus "complaints" and look in the CFPB complaint information.
You can ask an AI assistant to explain what an app's terms mean, but do not trust AI to tell you an app is safe. Check the official sources yourself.
Step by step:
- Download only from the official app store.
- Check the developer name matches the real company.
- Find the company's full name and partner bank on its own website.
- Check the bank on FDIC BankFind.
- Search for complaints, including on consumerfinance.gov.
Words to know:
- Developer: the company that made an app, shown in the app store listing.
- Terms of service: the rules and fees you agree to when you use an app.
Official sources:
- CFPB: Military financial lifecycle (complaints and rights)
- FDIC: Deposit insurance (BankFind)
Try it now: Run the five-point check on one money app you use or are thinking about. Write a yes or no next to each point.
You can now check whether a money app is real before you trust it with money.

check.q: What is the first point of the five-point app check?
options: Read online reviews only
Download only from the official app store, from the right developer
Check how pretty the app looks
Ask the app's chat bot if it is safe
check.why: Fake apps copy real ones, so you start by getting the real app from the official store.

check.q: An AI assistant says a new money app is "definitely safe". What do you do?
options: Put all your savings in it
Share the app with friends
Skip the other checks
Run the five-point check yourself on official sources
check.why: AI cannot confirm an app is safe for sure; you check official sources yourself.

lessons.title: Lesson 5: Locking down your money accounts
lessons.text:
Lesson 5 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Turn on the main security settings in a money app.
This lesson builds toward: In one money app, you will turn on two-step verification and payment alerts and remove unknown devices, without sharing any password or code.
Treat your money accounts like a secure area: layers of protection. Use a strong, unique password for each money account, and turn on two-step verification so a code or app is needed to log in.
Turn on alerts so the app tells you about every payment, login or change to your details. Fast alerts let you stop fraud early.
Never share a login code with anyone, even someone who says they are from the bank, VA or the app. Real companies do not ask for it. Never type passwords or full account numbers into an AI assistant.
Step by step:
- Set a strong, unique password.
- Turn on two-step verification in the app's security settings.
- Turn on alerts for payments, logins and changes.
- Check your linked devices and remove any you do not know.
- Promise yourself: never share a login code.
Words to know:
- Two-step verification: a second check, like a code or app approval, needed to log in.
- Alert: a message the app sends when something happens in your account.
Try it now: Open the security settings in one money app. Turn on two-step verification and payment alerts, and remove any device you do not recognize.
You can now set up the main security settings that protect a money account.

options: To get advertising
To share your balance with friends
To spot and stop fraud early
To make the app faster
check.why: Alerts tell you about each payment so you can catch fraud quickly.

check.q: In your app's security settings you see a device you do not recognize. What do you do?
options: Remove it and change your password
Leave it; it is probably fine
Turn off two-step verification
Post a screenshot online
check.why: An unknown device could be someone else in your account, so you remove it and secure the account.

lessons.title: Lesson 6: Spotting and reporting fintech scams
lessons.text:
Lesson 6 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Spot the warning signs of a fintech scam and know where to report it.
This lesson builds toward: Given a message, call or offer about money, you will identify the warning signs of a fintech scam and report it to the right place, sharing no codes and paying nothing.
The FTC warns that only scammers demand payment in crypto, only scammers guarantee profits or big returns, and a job that asks you to pay a crypto fee upfront is a scam. Romance contacts who offer investing tips are also a warning sign.
Scammers also pretend to be the bank, a government agency or the VA and say your money is at risk. AI lets them write perfect messages and even copy voices. Do not click their links or call back numbers they give you; use the number on the official website or your card.
To report: file a complaint about a financial product with the CFPB at consumerfinance.gov or by phone, and report fraud to the FTC at ReportFraud.ftc.gov. Tell your bank right away if money left your account.
Step by step:
- Watch for: crypto payment demands, guaranteed returns, upfront fees, urgent "your money is at risk" calls.
- Stop. Do not click, pay or share codes.
- Call the company on a number from its official website or your card.
- Tell your bank at once if money moved.
- Report to the CFPB or ReportFraud.ftc.gov.
Words to know:
- Impostor scam: when a scammer pretends to be a company, agency or person you trust.
- Guaranteed returns: a promise of profit with no risk; real investments never promise this.
Official sources:
- FTC: What to know about cryptocurrency and scams
- CFPB: Military financial lifecycle (submit a complaint)
Try it now: Final task: make your one-page Fintech Safety Card for one app: what it does and how it uses AI, whether your money is insured and how you checked, the security settings you turned on, three scam warning signs, and where you would report a problem.
You can now understand how a money app works, check and secure it, and spot and report fintech scams.
How your final task is checked:
What we look at Not yet Meets Exceeds What it does and how it uses AI The card does not say what the app does or how it uses AI. The card names the kind of fintech and one way the app uses AI. It also says what to do if the app's AI makes a wrong decision. Insurance checked Says the money is insured with no check, or guesses. Names the partner bank and whether it is FDIC-insured, checked on BankFind. Notes which parts of the balance are or are not covered and where that was confirmed. Security settings No security settings turned on. Two-step verification and payment alerts on, and unknown devices removed. Also lists one more setting turned on, such as a card lock or spending limit. Scam signs and reporting Fewer than three warning signs, or no place to report. Three scam warning signs and where to report a problem. Includes how to call the company back on a trusted number. App checked The app was not checked before use. The five-point check was done with yes or no for each point. The learner explains what they would do if any point was a no. To pass: Meets or Exceeds on every row. If a row is Not yet, fix that part and try again.

check.q: Which is a fintech scam warning sign?
options: A monthly statement you expected
A bank branch's posted hours
A receipt for something you bought
Pressure to move your money fast to a "safe" account
check.why: Rushing you to move money to a "safe" account is a classic impostor scam.

check.q: You get a text from "your bank" with a link to fix a problem. What do you do?
options: Tap the link and log in
Do not tap it; call the bank on the number on its official website or your card
Reply with your account number
Forward it to friends
check.why: You contact the company yourself using a number you trust, not one in the message.
